analysis.one_liner: Requires a suicide-prevention hotline label on every firearm sold in America.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sell a firearm unless the gun, its packaging, or its papers carry a clear label in English and Spanish with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline phone number and a warning triangle. Selling an unlabeled gun would count as a consumer product safety violation, with the same civil and criminal penalties that apply to unsafe products. Gun makers and dealers would have had two years after passage to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearm buyers and their families. More than half of gun deaths in the United States are suicides, often decided in moments of crisis; a warning label on the weapon itself reaches the person holding it at the moment of highest risk. It costs taxpayers nothing.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits manufacturers and retailers from selling any firearm without a clear, conspicuous label in English and Spanish carrying the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline toll-free number and a warning triangle.
Puts the label on the firearm or its packaging and included descriptive material, so the crisis-line number is in hand at the moment a gun is purchased and handled.
Enforces the requirement under existing Consumer Product Safety Act penalty provisions, which include civil fines and criminal penalties, and applies it to gun dealers as well as manufacturers.
Gives manufacturers and retailers a two-year runway after enactment to meet the labeling requirement.
Overcomes the current exclusion of firearms from the Consumer Product Safety Act so the labeling rule can actually apply to guns.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and federally licensed dealers bear the cost of designing and attaching labels, printing packaging and materials, and the risk of penalties for selling unlabeled guns. The cost is modest per unit but the bill sets a precedent for regulating firearms as consumer products.

drawbacks.text: The requirement is a label only; it does not fund crisis services, add waiting periods, or remove guns from anyone, so critics could reasonably argue it is a modest step whose real-world effect on suicide rates is unproven.

The bill attaches Consumer Product Safety Act penalties, including civil fines and criminal penalties for willful violations, to sales of unlabeled firearms, creating compliance and enforcement exposure for small dealers as well as large manufacturers.
Compliance takes effect only two years after enactment, so even if it had passed, no label would have appeared on new guns for two years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: the Lifeline number printed on the gun itself reaches a person at the moment a firearm is in their hands during a suicidal crisis, at essentially no cost to the public. The cost to manufacturers and dealers is small and the bill allowed two years to comply. The honest caveat is that a printed label is a low-cost intervention whose impact on suicide deaths is uncertain; it is a floor, not a comprehensive prevention program. On balance the burden falls on a profitable industry while the benefit accrues to gun owners' families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and sent to a subcommittee, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Julia Brownley introduced the Gun Suicide Prevention Act in the House on September 14, 2023, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Moulton, Napolitano, Grijalva, and Tlaib.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it stayed.
The bill gathered 20 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the committee never acted on it and it never reached the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers and sellers, who avoided a labeling mandate and any precedent for treating guns as consumer products; anyone at risk of gun suicide gained nothing because the label never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and sellers; no one else

industries.note: They would have had to design, produce, and attach hotline labels to every gun and its packaging, and face product-safety penalties for violations. The direct cost per unit is small, but the industry's resistance to any consumer-product-style regulation of firearms is what kept the bill dormant, and that resistance runs against the public's interest in reaching people at risk of suicide.

The bill explicitly covers dealers, so shops selling unlabeled guns would face fines and potential penalties. Compliance is inexpensive, so the material effect is modest; the industry's gain from the bill's death is avoiding the precedent rather than the sticker cost.
